html:
Henrik Ibsen was a Norwegian playwright, born in Skien in 1828, often called the father of modern drama.

He began with plays drawn from Norwegian history and the verse dramas Brand and Peer Gynt. Living abroad in Italy and Germany for 27 years, he then wrote plays of everyday middle-class life that exposed lies about money, marriage and duty: A Doll's House, Ghosts, An Enemy of the People, Hedda Gabler.

His plays shocked audiences, especially Nora walking out on her family, and were banned or rewritten in some places. They changed theatre across Europe and influenced writers such as Shaw and Chekhov. He came home to Kristiania, now Oslo, in 1891 as a national figure in Norway.
